assets.scenario_setup: Jordan, sixteen, just got a C-minus on a French II quiz and announced he is 'just not a languages person' and wants to drop the class. You are his older sister Maya, home for the weekend. Jordan's self-talk is a textbook entity-theory response: a setback read as evidence of a fixed ceiling. You have one conversation to reshape how he reads the failure before he emails the counselor.
dialogue: Jordan: I don't know why I try. The teacher said my accent is 'developing,' which is code for terrible.
Maya: Developing is literally the point. French is a skill you are building, not an asset you were issued at birth.
Jordan: Easy for you to say. You got A's in Spanish without trying.
Maya: I studied every morning for a year and still butchered the subjunctive. The grade came after the grind, not instead of it.
Jordan: So what do I do? Memorize the verb charts for the retest so I can get a B and look normal?
Maya: That is a performance goal: get the letter, prove you are not dumb. Here is a different one: by June, be able to hold a real conversation at a bakery counter in Paris.
Jordan: A conversation? That is way scarier than a quiz.
Maya: Scarier means it is the right size. A goal that asks you to grow is supposed to stretch you. The C is not a verdict; it is information about where the stretch should go.
Jordan: So retaking the quiz just to check the box is the trap.
Maya: Now you are seeing it. Want me to quiz you on the verb charts tonight, and after that we practice ordering a pain au chocolat?
choices: Exactly. Let us replace 'get an A on the retest' with 'speak French well enough to order lunch in Paris by June' and start tonight with verb charts and an accent drill.

You are right that your ceiling may be lower than your classmates'. Let us just try to pass the class and get the credit over with.
Fine, drop the class. Mom and Dad will be upset, but if French makes you feel bad about yourself, protecting your self-image matters more.

assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 reframes the setback under an incremental theory: the C becomes guidepost information, and the goal shifts from proving ability to developing it, the pattern Dweck's junior high studies showed produced higher transfer scores and longer persistence. Choice 1 is a performance-goal pep talk that ties Jordan's worth to fixed smartness and pressures him toward easy successes. Choice 2 endorses the entity theory, telling a capable student she has hit her ceiling, which Dweck's data show produces helpless responses to difficulty. Choice 3 opts out of mastery entirely, treating self-image as something to protect instead of competence as something to build.

assets.topic: The three laws of mastery
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom-style evidence wall in a behavioral-science archive. The player drags each exhibit under one of three law placards.
assets.player_mission: Read each finding and sort it under the law of mastery it best supports: mastery is a mindset, mastery is a pain, or mastery is an asymptote. File all seven exhibits correctly on the evidence wall.
key_concepts: Mastery abides by three laws: mastery is a mindset, mastery is a pain, and mastery is an asymptote.
Flow is essential to mastery but does not guarantee it, because flow happens in a moment while mastery unfolds over months, years, sometimes decades.
Dweck's research shows that beliefs about the nature of ability determine how we interpret experiences and can set boundaries on accomplishment.
Anders Ericsson's research holds that many characteristics once believed to reflect innate talent are actually the results of intense practice for a minimum of ten years.
At West Point, the best predictor of which cadets survived Beast Barracks was grit, defined as perseverance and passion for long-term goals.
Daniel Chambliss, after a three-year study of Olympic swimmers, called excellence's dependence on routine preparation 'the mundanity of excellence.'
The West Point researchers argued that in every field, grit may be as essential as talent to high accomplishment.
An asymptote is a straight line that a curve approaches but never quite reaches.
A critic wrote that for Cézanne, the synthesis of a design was an asymptote toward which he was forever approaching without ever quite reaching it.
Tiger Woods says he can and must become better, and he understands that mastery will always hover beyond his grasp; the joy is in the pursuit more than the realization.

assets.topic: The mindset reset
assets.visual_frame_description: A Portland accounting firm's break room, where Marcus, a 34-year-old accountant, stares at a mock exam marked 61 percent. His colleague watches as Marcus re-reads his old notes and retakes the same practice exam rather than tackling unfamiliar problems. The failed analytics module is scheduled to be dropped from his plan next week.
assets.player_mission: You are Marcus's mentor. First, identify the self-theory and goal pattern that is derailing his study plan. Then, one week later, give him guidance grounded in Dweck's findings that can shift his mindset before he withdraws from the module.
key_concepts: Dweck's signature insight is that what people believe shapes what they achieve.
Entity theorists believe intelligence exists within us in a finite supply that we cannot increase; incremental theorists believe it can increase with effort.
If you believe intelligence is a fixed quantity, every educational and professional encounter becomes a measure of how much you have.
If you believe intelligence can increase, the same encounters become opportunities for growth.
Entity theorists want to look like masters without expending the effort to attain mastery.
In Dweck's study, students who subscribed to fixed brain-power gave up quickly on tough problems and blamed their lack of intelligence.
Students with a more expansive mindset kept working, deployed far more inventive strategies, and did not blame anything for their difficulty.
The young people with an expansive mindset recognized that setbacks are inevitable on the road to mastery and can be guideposts for the journey.
With a learning goal, students do not have to feel they are already good at something in order to hang in and keep trying.
Dweck says effort is one of the things that gives meaning to life because it means you care about something and are willing to work for it.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests Dweck's entity-versus-incremental self-theory distinction: a fixed belief converts failure into evidence of incapacity, while a malleable belief converts failure into guidance. Her studies of fifth- and sixth-graders show the growth-oriented view produces persistence, inventive strategies, and mastery-oriented responses to adversity.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Mastery is a mindset. Dweck's self-theories show that believing intelligence is a fixed entity turns every setback into a verdict on your worth, while believing it can grow turns setbacks into guideposts, and the goal a person chooses follows from whichever belief he holds.
assets.stage_1_observation: Marcus, a 34-year-old accountant at a mid-sized firm in Portland, just scored 61 percent on the mock exam for the new data-analytics module of the CPA credential. In the break room he tells a colleague, 'I have never been good with software, and clearly I never will be. I would rather stick to what I am already good at.' His colleague notices that Marcus keeps re-reading his old notes and re-taking the same practice exam instead of solving unfamiliar problems.
assets.stage_1_question: What belief-and-goal pattern is holding Marcus back?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Marcus holds an entity theory of intelligence: he treats the module as a measure of a fixed ability he cannot increase. His behavior shows a shift toward performance goals that demand easy successes he can already hit, which is why he repeats familiar practice exams; Dweck's research shows this pattern converts the setback into proof of incapacity and drives helpless responses.
assets.stage_2_intervention: One week later Marcus tells you he is dropping the analytics module. Which guidance, grounded in Dweck's findings, should you give him to change course?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Recast the goal from performance to learning: reframe the module as a chance to develop a new capability, like building strength, treat the failed mock exam as a guidepost, and have him practice on problems just beyond his current level. Dweck's studies show learning-goal students hang in, try more solutions, and outscore performance-goal students on novel problems, so the module becomes an opportunity for growth instead of a verdict.

assets.topic: Grit at Beast Barracks
assets.visual_frame_description: Week six of Cadet Basic Training at West Point: a dusty parade ground at dusk, cadets in gray T-shirts running the same footwork drill for the fifth time. Cadet Rivera, a star athlete, slumps against a wall during a rest break; Cadet Osei, unremarkable on paper, quietly keeps drilling. Behind them, the long gray line of the Academy library rises against the Hudson River.
assets.player_mission: You serve on the Academy's retention research team. First, predict which cadet profile the West Point grit study says will persist, and why. Then, in week seven, recommend how to respond when the promising cadet wants to quit.
key_concepts: Each summer about 1,200 young American men and women arrive at West Point, and before any classroom work they endure seven weeks of Cadet Basic Training known as Beast Barracks.
By the time the summer ends, one in twenty of these talented, dedicated young adults has dropped out.
The West Point study team included scholars from West Point, the University of Pennsylvania, and the University of Michigan.
The best predictor of cadet success was their rating on grit, defined as perseverance and passion for long-term goals.
Physical strength, intellect, leadership ability, and well-roundedness were not the predictors that distinguished those who stayed.
The same researchers found that grittiness, rather than IQ or standardized test scores, is the most accurate predictor of college grades.
The researchers wrote that working longer without switching objectives may be less perceptible than working harder, and that grit may be as essential as talent to high accomplishment.
Ericsson's research holds that many characteristics once believed to reflect innate talent are actually the results of intense practice for a minimum of ten years.
Daniel Chambliss's three-year study of Olympic swimmers found that the best spent the most time and effort on the mundane activities that readied them for races.
Moments of flow in the course of pursuing excellence can help people through the rough parts of mastery.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the second law of mastery, that mastery is a pain. The West Point study showed that grit, defined as perseverance and passion for long-term goals, predicted which cadets endured Beast Barracks better than strength, intellect, or leadership, and Ericsson's expert-performance research links achievement to years of effortful, often unglamorous practice.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Mastery is a pain. The path to becoming ever better at something you care about requires difficult, all-consuming effort over a long time, and the West Point evidence shows the trait that carries people through is grit: perseverance and passion for long-term goals.
assets.stage_1_observation: It is week six of Beast Barracks. Cadet Rivera, a gifted athlete with a 4.0 GPA, is wilting under the routine of marching drills, uniform inspections, and demerit paperwork. Cadet Osei, average on every physical and academic metric so far, wakes early, drills the same footwork nightly, and has never missed a study session. On the latest fitness test the two nearly match. The retention committee must predict who is more likely to be standing in the long gray line in four years.
assets.stage_1_question: Which cadet does the grit research predict will persist, and why?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Cadet Osei, because the best predictor of staying was not physical strength, intellect, leadership, or well-roundedness, but grit. Osei shows the perseverance and passion for long-term goals that keeps her working the same routine without switching objectives, the trait the same researchers found predicted college grades better than IQ or test scores.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Week seven: Cadet Rivera, facing her first demerit, says, 'Maybe the Army just is not for me.' The retention team wants your recommendation on how to respond, given that mastery hurts.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Keep Rivera oriented toward the long-term goal rather than the immediate setback: acknowledge that difficulty is normal on the path to mastery, since expert performance grows out of intense practice over a minimum of ten years. Help her identify which moments put her in flow so she knows what she is working toward, and set the expectation that progress comes from working longer without switching objectives, not from sudden talent.

assets.topic: The mastery asymptote
assets.visual_frame_description: A busy pastry kitchen in San Francisco the night of a regional competition. Elena, a 41-year-old pastry chef, stares at her winning mille-feuille on the pass counter while the trophy sits untouched beside it. In the corner of the frame, a math textbook diagram shows a curve approaching a horizontal asymptote that it never touches, and a Cézanne landscape hangs on the wall.
assets.player_mission: You are Elena's mentor. First, explain to her sous-chef why Elena's dissatisfaction is not a failure of appreciation. Then, recommend which of two career paths she should choose and what she should expect to feel along it.
key_concepts: An asymptote is a straight line that a curve approaches but never quite reaches.
University of Chicago economist David Galenson, who studied the careers of artists, linked Cézanne's most enduring late paintings to his endless attempts to realize his best work.
A critic wrote that for Cézanne the ultimate synthesis of a design was never revealed in a flash but approached with infinite precautions, forever approaching without ever quite reaching it.
Mastery is impossible to realize fully: you can approach it, home in on it, and get really, really close, but never touch it.
Tiger Woods has said flatly that he can, and must, become better, whether as an amateur, after his best outing, or at the end of his finest season.
Woods understands that mastery will always hover beyond his grasp.
The mastery asymptote is a source of frustration because it asks why you would reach for something you can never fully attain.
The mastery asymptote is also a source of allure because the joy is in the pursuit more than the realization.
In the end, mastery attracts precisely because mastery eludes.
Robert Reich advises figuring out what you want to be really good at, knowing you will never really satisfy yourself that you have made it, and accepting that that is okay.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the third law of mastery, the asymptote: the goal recedes as you approach it, generating frustration and allure in equal measure. Pink grounds the law in Cézanne's endless stalking of an unreachable synthesis and Tiger Woods's insistence that he can and must improve even though mastery will always hover beyond his grasp.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Mastery is an asymptote: like a curve approaching a horizontal line, you can home in on mastery but never touch it. Cézanne stalked his ideal synthesis for decades without reaching it, and Tiger Woods knows his best will always hover beyond his grasp; the frustration and the allure come from the same unattainability.
assets.stage_1_observation: Elena, a 41-year-old pastry chef, has just won a regional competition for her signature mille-feuille. At the celebration she looks uneasy and tells her sous-chef, 'It is good, but I can already see the next version. The caramel needs one more degree of patience.' Her sous-chef is baffled: 'You just won first place. Why do you look like you lost?'
assets.stage_1_question: Is Elena's dissatisfaction a failure of appreciation or the signature of the mastery asymptote?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: It is the mastery asymptote at work. Elena's joy is in the pursuit more than the realization, because mastery attracts precisely because mastery eludes. Cézanne approached his ultimate synthesis forever without quite reaching it, and Tiger Woods says he can and must become better even as he knows mastery will always hover beyond his grasp.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Elena's mentor offers two paths: cap her ambition and compete at a comfortable level where she always wins, or keep pushing toward a 'perfect' mille-feuille she concedes she will never wholly produce. Which path should she choose, and what should she expect to feel along the way?

That is the position Robert Reich describes: figure out what you want to be really good at, know you will never fully make it, and accept that that is okay.

assets.topic: Goldilocks tasks and the positive Sawyer Effect
assets.visual_frame_description: A hospital corridor where a cleaner in navy scrubs stops to chat with a recovering patient and then straightens a nurse's supply cart; a second panel shows an Ericsson manager in a one-on-one meeting, and a third shows a calibration dial labeled 'challenge' being tuned between 'boredom' and 'anxiety.' assets.player_mission: Classify each workplace tactic as a Goldilocks task, positive-Sawyer-Effect job sculpting, or broader flow-friendly structuring. Sort all seven tactic cards into the correct columns on the strategy board.
key_concepts: Organizations that increase flow-friendliness typically use Goldilocks tasks: challenges that are neither too hot nor too cold, neither overly difficult nor overly simple.
A frequent source of workplace frustration is the mismatch between what people must do and what people can do.
When what people must do exceeds their capabilities, the result is anxiety.
When what people must do falls short of their capabilities, the result is boredom.
Csikszentmihalyi titled his first book on autotelic experiences Beyond Boredom and Anxiety.
The positive side of the Sawyer Effect runs the current in the other direction, turning work into play.

Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton studied hospital cleaners, nurses, and hairdressers, finding that some cleaners took on tasks such as chatting with patients and helping nurses' jobs go more smoothly.
Adding more absorbing challenges increased the cleaners' satisfaction and boosted their own views of their skills.
Wrzesniewski and Dutton write that even in low-autonomy jobs, employees can create new domains for mastery.
A study of 11,000 industrial scientists and engineers in the United States found that the desire for intellectual challenge was the best predictor of productivity.

assets.topic: Forty-eight hours without flow
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1970s psychology laboratory at the University of Chicago: participants sit in a drab waiting room filling out Experience Sampling Method booklets. One man rubs a headache beneath fluorescent lights, a woman stares at the clock, and a handwritten sign on the door reads 'No Play Allowed.' A DSM-IV symptom checklist sits beside the researcher's notebook.
assets.player_mission: You are the lab's attending researcher. First, diagnose what is happening to the participants of Csikszentmihalyi's two-day experiment. Then, propose a workplace package that prevents the same danger signs in employees.
key_concepts: Generalized anxiety disorder is a mental illness that afflicts roughly 3 percent of the adult population.

According to the DSM-IV, the presence of any three of six symptoms, such as restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, indicates a potentially serious problem.
In the early 1970s Csikszentmihalyi asked people to record all the noninstrumental things they did, small activities undertaken not out of obligation but because they enjoyed them.
He then instructed participants to act in a normal way while doing nothing that was play or noninstrumental.
One woman enjoyed washing dishes because it gave her something constructive to do and time to fantasize free of guilt, but she could wash dishes only when absolutely necessary.
Even at the end of the first day, participants noticed an increased sluggishness about their behavior.
Participants complained of headaches, difficulty concentrating, and thoughts that wandered round in circles without getting anywhere.
Some felt sleepy while others were too agitated to sleep.
After just two days of deprivation, the general deterioration in mood was so advanced that prolonging the experiment would have been unadvisable.
Flow is not a nicety; it is a necessity, the oxygen of the soul.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the chapter's 'oxygen of the soul' experiment: scrubbing every play-like, noninstrumental activity from daily life produced headaches, irritability, concentration trouble, and sleep disruption within two days, a mood profile resembling generalized anxiety disorder. The finding supports Pink's claim that flow is a psychological necessity rather than a luxury.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Flow is the oxygen of the soul. assets.column_b_label: Autonomy over technique — how you do it
assets.column_c_label: Autonomy over time — when you do it

rows.label: Dario, a customer-success manager, chooses the healthcare accounts he will lead this quarter instead of receiving an assigned roster
Nina, a data analyst, rewrites the firm's required dashboard template into a cleaner structure she finds easier to maintain
Marcus, an engineer, starts work at 7 a.m., takes a long midday break for his run, and logs off at 6 p.m., because his firm values only deadlines
Elena volunteers to own the new client-onboarding brief instead of waiting for her supervisor to delegate it
Hassan swaps the mandated morning stand-up for an asynchronous written update he produces whenever his focus is sharpest
Priya picks a cello teacher whose method matches how she learns best, ignoring the conservatory's recommended syllabus

distractors: Choosing which accounts to lead is time autonomy, because it depends on scheduling your quarter.
Swapping the stand-up for an asynchronous update is task autonomy, because it changes what gets produced.
Rewriting the dashboard template is time autonomy, because the rewrite takes extra time to complete.
assets.explanation: The guide distinguishes four autonomous freedoms — what you do (task), when you do it (time), how you do it (technique), and with whom you do it (team). Rows one and four change the work itself, so they exercise task autonomy. Rows two and six alter the method of the work, so they exercise technique autonomy. Rows three and five alter the schedule of the work, so they exercise time autonomy. The correct answer for the lead row is 'a' because choosing which accounts to lead is a choice about what work gets done — the defining feature of task autonomy.

assets.topic: Piloting a FedEx Day Without Strangling It
assets.visual_frame_description: A Columbus insurance office on a Thursday: four teams huddle around whiteboards, one group building a working shelf-appraisal tool with real momentum. In a corner office, a manager taps a mandatory check-in timer on his phone while a ranked demo board with a perk-prize line hangs over the room.
assets.player_mission: Identify which detail is strangling the FedEx Day pilot, then choose how the CEO should run the initiative so it honors the autonomy it is meant to grant. Win the battle by keeping the burst of autonomy unscripted.
key_concepts: A FedEx Day is a one-day burst of autonomy in which employees tackle any problem they want and show results by the end of twenty-four hours.
The guide asks whether initiatives like FedEx Days, 20 percent time, and ROWE would work in the reader's organization.
The guide also asks for ideas that would bring out more Type I behavior in the workplace.
20 percent time lets employees spend one day in five working on any project they choose.
A results-only work environment removes schedules; employees just have to get their work done.
Type I behavior is powered by the innate need to direct our own lives, to learn and create new things, and to do better.
The guide asks how well a job meets the need for baseline rewards — salary, benefits, and a few perks.
The guide asks readers to recall the seven deadly flaws of carrots and sticks in action.
The guide's introduction argues that ideas come to life when talked over in person — that the world changes conversation by conversation.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests whether a manager understands what makes an autonomy initiative a Motivation 3.0 practice: FedEx Days work by letting employees choose the problem and own the process, and control mechanisms stapled on top of the day defeat its purpose. The distinction between engagement and compliance runs through the book's treatment of autonomy as an innate psychological need.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests the discussion guide's question of whether initiatives like FedEx Days, 20 percent time, and ROWE would work in an organization — specifically, whether the manager understands that a FedEx Day is a burst of autonomy and will strangle it with contingencies.
assets.stage_1_observation: At a Columbus insurance company, CEO Marta Villanueva launches her first FedEx Day after reading the discussion guide: four teams of twenty get a Thursday to tackle any problem they want, with demos due Friday afternoon. By lunch, three teams are building a shelf-appraisal tool with real promise; one manager, however, schedules mandatory check-ins every two hours, orders his team to work on his pet project, and announces the Friday demos will be ranked with the bottom team losing a monthly perk.
assets.stage_1_question: During the pilot, which detail most undermines the FedEx Day's motivational logic?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The manager's behavior: the two-hour check-ins, the assigned pet project, and the threatened loss of a perk convert the day of autonomous problem-choosing into precisely the controlled, contingent environment the initiative is meant to escape. A FedEx Day is a burst of autonomy — employees tackle any problem they want and show results within twenty-four hours — and that one team is not running the day at all.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Marta must decide how to proceed: (A) cancel the program because one day of self-chosen projects wastes productive time; (B) formalize it — require measurable output, tie the day to a bonus, and pre-approve every project; (C) keep the day unscripted, protect the teams from managerial oversight, let the Friday demos stand as the only yardstick, and ask whether ROWE or 20 percent time deserves a pilot next. Which step is most consistent with the guide's autonomy question?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Option C. The guide treats FedEx Days, 20 percent time, and ROWE as vehicles for autonomy — over task, time, technique, and team — so protecting self-direction and letting each team own its problem, pace, and method is the point. Option A overreacts to a single piloted day, and option B wraps a freedom-granting initiative in the contingencies it exists to remove.

The player must judge each behavior's motivational fuel.
assets.player_mission: Read each behavior and sort it as Type I behavior, Type X behavior, or a neutral everyday preference outside the book's two types. Complete the matrix to finish the chapter's self-audit.
key_concepts: Type I behavior is built around intrinsic rather than extrinsic motivators.
Type I behavior is powered by our innate need to direct our own lives, to learn and create new things, and to do better by ourselves and our world.
Type X behavior is fueled more by extrinsic desires than intrinsic ones.
Type X behavior concerns itself less with the inherent satisfaction of an activity and more with the external rewards to which that activity leads.
The guide asks readers to consider whether they are more Type I or Type X.
The guide asks readers to classify three people in their lives and to explain the reasoning behind the classification.
Question eighteen asks whether a parent's home environment promotes more Type I or Type X behavior in children.
Question seventeen asks whether education is too Type X and how to reconcile intrinsic motivation with accountability.
The guide's flow question asks where and when the reader last experienced flow and how to tweak a role to bring on more optimal experiences.
Hobbies pursued for their own sake are everyday expressions of intrinsic motivation.
assets.theory_summary: This task tests the Type I/Type X distinction — intrinsic versus extrinsic motivational orientation — by classifying real-life behaviors into the two camps the discussion guide asks readers to examine in themselves and others. credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.question: Read each behavior and sort it into Type I behavior, Type X behavior, or a neutral preference that the book's two-type distinction does not classify.
assets.column_a_label: Type I — built around intrinsic motivators
assets.column_b_label: Type X — fueled more by extrinsic desires and external rewards
assets.column_c_label: Neutral — an everyday preference with no clear motivational orientation

rows.label: Kofi practices drums nightly for the pure satisfaction of getting better, not for any trophy
Leah chose her job chiefly because of the bonus structure and the promotion ladder
Taking a lunch break because you enjoy the sandwich you packed
Simone volunteers at the food bank on Saturdays because she loves the work itself
Aidan checks his sales rankings hourly because the public board gratifies him
Choosing the window seat because you like the view

distractors: Volunteering at a food bank is Type X because volunteers receive no payment, which proves the activity runs on reputation instead.
Practicing drums nightly for satisfaction is Type X because drumming builds a skill that could someday earn money.
A job chosen for its bonus structure is Type I because receiving a bonus is a form of recognition and recognition is intrinsic.
assets.explanation: Type I behavior is powered by intrinsic motivators — the inherent satisfaction of the activity itself, the pull to learn and create — which is what Kofi's drumming and Simone's volunteering show. Type X behavior is fueled more by extrinsic desires and oriented to the external rewards an activity leads to, which is what Leah's job choice and Aidan's ranking-checking show. The neutral column holds ordinary preferences — a packed sandwich, a window seat — that involve no intrinsic-versus-extrinsic tension and that the guide's two-type frame does not classify. The correct answer for the lead row is 'a' because Kofi's motivation is the inherent satisfaction of getting better, the signature of Type I behavior.

assets.topic: Rolling Out the Type I/Type X Assessment
assets.visual_frame_description: An HR office at a 400-person retail analytics firm: a large screen shows a completion dashboard ranking departments by assessment click-through, with a catered-lunch prize banner on top. Head of people Ade Adeyemi watches employees clicking through the free Type I/Type X assessment in under thirty seconds while a few whisper about surveillance.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose why the mandatory, ranked rollout of a personal self-assessment hollowed it out, then choose the rollout that matches the chapter's invitation to find out more about yourself. Win the battle by respecting the assessment's voluntary, self-directed purpose.
key_concepts: The final chapter asks readers a direct question: are you Type I or Type X?
The chapter directs readers to a free online assessment at www.danpink.com/drive.html.
The assessment is framed as a tool for self-discovery about one's own motivation.
Drive Times is a free quarterly e-mail newsletter on the science and practice of human motivation.
Type I behavior is built around intrinsic rather than extrinsic motivators.
Type X behavior is fueled more by extrinsic desires than intrinsic ones.
A mandatory, ranked rollout converts a self-directed resource into a contingent, externally monitored task.
The chapter's heading frames its content as being about yourself and this topic — personal reflection plus subject learning.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests whether a leader can create conditions for genuine self-discovery — the chapter's invitation to find out more about yourself and this topic — instead of extrinsic compliance. The assessment is a free, optional resource in the text, so coercive rollouts contradict its motivational spirit.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests the final chapter's resources: a free online assessment for determining whether a reader is Type I or Type X, and the invitation to find out more about yourself and this topic — which requires voluntary, self-directed engagement rather than compliance-driven completion.
assets.stage_1_observation: Ade Adeyemi, head of people at a 400-person retail analytics firm, runs a Motivation Month: every employee must complete the free Type I/Type X assessment before Friday, and the HR dashboard ranks each department by completion percentage, with the winning department earning a catered lunch. By Thursday, completion sits at 96 percent, but a teammate tells Ade that people are clicking answers in thirty seconds to get it over with, and a few are muttering about surveillance.
assets.stage_1_question: The assessment is being completed, but the exercise is hollow. In this chapter's terms, why?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The mandatory, ranked, prize-linked rollout turned a free, self-paced assessment designed for personal insight into another contingent, externally monitored task — completion became an extrinsic chore, and the public ranking made it a competition for a prize rather than an occasion for reflection. The chapter frames the assessment as a resource for finding out more about yourself, which requires voluntary engagement.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Ade wants a do-over. Which plan best matches the chapter's framing? (A) Keep the completion quota but change the prize to a half-day off; (B) drop the quota and the ranking, host the assessment as a voluntary lunch-and-learn where people score themselves privately and share only if they choose, and link the free newsletter for anyone who wants to keep learning; (C) reprimand the employees who dismissed the assessment as surveillance and require written reflection essays from everyone else. Which option do you choose?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Option B. The chapter positions the assessment as a free resource the reader chooses to use, so a voluntary, private, self-directed format preserves its intrinsic purpose. Option A keeps an external contingency and just swaps the prize, and option C introduces punitive control that directly contradicts the chapter's invitation to find out more about yourself — the very opposite of what the resource is for.

You chose your side job because it pays the best, even though you dread the work

Caring that salary is adequate and equitable is a baseline concern rather than an orientation: the glossary says Type I's and Type X's both care about money, and an inadequate or inequitable baseline makes motivation of any sort extremely difficult. The correct answer for the lead row is 'a' because the craft itself pulls you — the defining feature of Type I behavior.

assets.topic: Drive Times: Making Motivation Learning Voluntary
assets.visual_frame_description: A Portland nonprofit's staff office: a shared tracker on the wall titled Newsletter Takeaways, filled with tautological bullet points, while two program officers wordlessly forward the quarterly e-mail newsletter Drive Times to an archive folder. Executive director Lena Cho looks on, puzzled that required learning produced resentment.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose why the mandatory newsletter requirement killed curiosity, then choose the redesign that treats ongoing motivation learning as the voluntary, self-directed pursuit the chapter describes. Win the battle to bring Drive Times back to life.
key_concepts: Drive Times is a free quarterly e-mail newsletter on the science and practice of human motivation.
The final chapter invites readers to find out more about themselves and the topic.
Continuous learning about motivation works best when it is voluntary and self-directed.
Requiring a subscription and mandated takeaways turns a learning resource into an extrinsic obligation.
Contingent requirements attached to learning tend to crowd out intrinsic curiosity.
The book offers a free online Type I/Type X assessment for personal use.
The book's overall stance is that there is a gap between what science knows and what organizations do.
Voluntary, social formats — like a coffee chat where people share what they found interesting — preserve autonomy.
External contingencies can convert an invitation to learn into a compliance artifact and feed resentment.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the chapter's invitation to keep learning about motivation science through free, self-directed resources — the assessment and Drive Times — and the damage done when a curiosity-offering is re-cast as a mandated, tracked obligation. The mechanism is the book's recurring claim that contingent controls can suppress the intrinsic interest they pretend to support.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests the final chapter's ongoing-learning resources — the free quarterly newsletter Drive Times on the science and practice of human motivation — and whether a leader treats continuing motivation education as an intrinsic pursuit or re-frames it as a compliance program.
assets.stage_1_observation: At a Portland nonprofit, executive director Lena Cho wants her staff to stay current on motivation science, so she requires every program officer to subscribe to the quarterly newsletter Drive Times and to paste three takeaways into a shared tracker each quarter. The tracker fills with tautological bullet points, and two officers quietly admit they forward the newsletter unread — the ritual is feeding resentment, not curiosity.
assets.stage_1_question: Why is the subscription requirement producing the opposite of continuous learning?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Requiring the subscription and the mandated takeaways reconfigured an invitation to learn — the chapter's promise of regular, free updates on the science and practice of human motivation — into an extrinsic obligation with a compliance artifact, the tracker. Contingent requirements attached to learning tend to crowd out the intrinsic curiosity the newsletter is meant to serve, so the ritual produced compliance and resentment.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Lena's options: (A) keep the tracker but grade the takeaways; (B) unsubscribe everyone and buy each officer a conference pass with a mandatory session schedule; (C) make learning voluntary and social — put one copy of the newsletter in the break room, let anyone who finds something interesting raise it in the standing Friday coffee chat, post the free assessment link for personal use, and let word of mouth carry it. Which option fits the chapter's spirit best?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Option C. The chapter frames these resources as free, optional, self-directed aids — find out more about yourself and this topic — so voluntary, social formats preserve autonomy and intrinsic interest. Options A and B retain contingent requirements, a graded tracker and a mandated conference schedule, that reproduce the compliance dynamic the chapter's framing is built to avoid.
